subject: math
title: Comparing Fractions and Decimals: Positive and Negative Numbers, Simplifying and Rounding
seo_title: Grade 7 Comparing Fractions and Decimals Worksheets: Negative Numbers, Simplifying, Rounding (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Read, represent, compare, and order positive and negative fractions and decimal numbers to thousandths, in various contexts
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 math worksheets for the Ontario curriculum: positive and negative fractions and decimals on a number line, comparing and ordering, simplifying fractions, numbers between two quantities, and rounding. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The farther left on the number line, the less the number, so −0.5 < −0.25.
key_sub: Compare decimals place by place, not by length: 0.5 = 0.50 > 0.45. Simplify a fraction by dividing both parts by their greatest common factor.
body_html:
Positive and negative fractions and decimals

Fractions and decimals can be negative too. On a number line, negative numbers are to the left of 0 (or below 0 on a vertical line, like a thermometer). −0.25 is read “negative twenty-five hundredths”.

Before you read a point, find what each space is worth: the difference between two labels ÷ the number of spaces between them.

Compare and order

The farther left a number is, the less it is. For two negative numbers, the one closer to 0 is greater.

To compare decimals, give them the same number of places: 0.5 = 0.50 > 0.45. To compare fractions, use a common denominator or write them as decimals: 38 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

Example 1

Order from least to greatest: −0.5, −34, 0.4, −0.25

−34 = −0.75. Start with the number farthest from 0 on the left: −0.75, then −0.5, then −0.25, then 0.4.

Answer: −34, −0.5, −0.25, 0.4

Simplify fractions

Divide the numerator and the denominator by their greatest common factor (GCF). The fraction keeps its value.

Example 2

Write 1824 in simplest form.

The GCF of 18 and 24 is 6. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4. (Dividing by 2 gives 912, which is not yet in simplest form.)

Answer: 34

Numbers in between

There is always another number between two different numbers. Add a zero to get more places, then pick a number in the middle.

Example 3

Find a number between −0.5 and −0.4.

Write −0.50 and −0.40. Any number of hundredths from 41 to 49, with the minus sign, is between them.

Answer: −0.45 (or −0.42, −0.48, …)

Round decimals

Look at the digit one place to the right of the place you are rounding to. 5 or more: round up. 4 or less: round down. For a negative number, round it as if it were positive, then keep the minus sign.

RoundLook atAnswer

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
−0.5 > −0.25 because 0.5 > 0.25Farther left is less: −0.5 < −0.25
0.45 > 0.5 because it has more digitsUse the same number of places: 0.45 < 0.50
Counting tick marks instead of spacesCount the spaces between labels: 4 spaces means fourths
Simplifying only the numerator: 1218 → 218Divide both parts by the GCF: 23
Rounding twice: 12.49 → 12.5 → 13Round the number you started with: 12

faq.q: What do Grade 7 students learn about fractions and decimals in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: Grade 7 students read, represent, compare and order positive and negative fractions and decimals to thousandths. They also simplify fractions, find a number between any two numbers, and round decimals to the nearest tenth, hundredth or whole number.
No. −0.5 is farther left on the number line, so −0.5 < −0.25, just as −0.5 °C is colder than −0.25 °C.

faq.q: How do you simplify a fraction?
faq.a: Divide the numerator and the denominator by their greatest common factor. For 18/24 the greatest common factor is 6, so 18/24 = 3/4.

faq.q: How do you round a negative decimal?
faq.a: Round it as if it were positive, then keep the minus sign. −2.46 rounded to the nearest tenth is −2.5, because 2.46 rounds to 2.5.

sets.title: Fractions and decimals on a number line

items.q: Which number is “negative two and three tenths”?
items.e: “Two and” is the whole number 2. “Three tenths” is 3 in the tenths place: 2.3. “Negative” adds the minus sign: −2.3.

items.q: Which number is “negative four hundredths”?
items.e: Hundredths take two places after the decimal point, so 4 hundredths is 0.04. With the sign: −0.04. −0.4 is four tenths.

items.q: Which number is “negative five and twelve thousandths”?
items.e: Thousandths take three places, so twelve thousandths is 0.012. Add the 5 ones and the sign: −5.012. −5.12 is five and twelve hundredths.

items.q: Which number is “negative three fifths”?
items.e: Three fifths is 35: 3 is the numerator and 5 is the denominator. With the sign: −35. −3.5 is three and five tenths.

items.q: Point A is at −0.75. Which fraction names the same point?
items.e: 0.75 = 75 hundredths = 75100 = 34. The point is negative, so A = −34. Do not drop the minus sign.

items.q: Which decimal names the same number as −25?
items.e: 25 = 410 = 0.4. So −25 = −0.4. −2.5 just puts the 2 and the 5 on each side of a decimal point.

items.q: Which decimal names the same number as −1 12?
items.e: 12 = 510 = 0.5, so −1 12 = −1.5. The denominator 2 does not become the digit 2.

items.q: What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 5 spaces between −0.5 and 0, so each tick mark is 0.1. A is 2 tick marks left of −0.5: −0.6, −0.7. A = −0.7. Going left makes a number less, so it is not −0.3.

items.q: What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 10 spaces between −2 and −1, so each tick mark is 0.1. A is 4 tick marks left of −1: −1.1, −1.2, −1.3, −1.4. A = −1.4. It is 6 tick marks right of −2, so it is not −1.6.

items.q: What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 10 spaces between −0.5 and −0.4, so each tick mark is 0.01. A is 3 tick marks left of −0.4: −0.41, −0.42, −0.43. A = −0.43. −0.47 is 3 tick marks from −0.5, the wrong end.

items.q: What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 4 equal spaces between −1 and 0, so each space is 14. A is 1 space left of 0: A = −14. Count the spaces, not the 3 tick marks in between (that gives thirds).

items.q: What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 3 equal spaces between whole numbers, so each space is 13. A is 2 spaces left of −1: −1 13, −1 23. A = −1 23. Do not forget the whole number: −23 is between −1 and 0.

items.q: What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 5 equal spaces between −1 and 0, so each space is 15. A is 3 spaces left of 0: A = −35. It is 2 spaces right of −1, so it is not −25.

items.q: Which point is at −1.25?
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 spaces, so each tick mark is 0.25. −1.25 is 1 tick mark left of −1. The point 1 tick mark right of −1 is −0.75. The answer is point C.

items.q: Which point is at −34?
items.e: Each space is 14. −34 is 3 spaces left of 0, which is 1 space right of −1. The answer is point D.

items.q: Which point is at −0.6?
items.e: There are 10 spaces between −1 and 0, so each tick mark is 0.1. −0.6 is 6 tick marks left of 0. −0.4 is only 4 tick marks left of 0. The answer is point B.

items.q: Which point is at −2 13?
items.e: Each space is 13. −2 13 is 1 space left of −2. −2 23 is 2 spaces left of −2, and −1 23 is 2 spaces left of −1. The answer is point A.

items.q: This vertical number line shows the water level of Lake Ontario compared with its usual level, in metres. What number is at point A?
items.e: There are 5 spaces between 0 and 0.5, so each tick mark is 0.1. A is 2 tick marks above −0.5: −0.4, −0.3. A = −0.3, so the lake is 0.3 m below its usual level. Going up makes a number greater, so it is not −0.7.

items.q: This thermometer shows the temperature at a ski hill near Collingwood. What is the temperature?
items.e: The labels count by 1, and there are 2 spaces between labels, so each tick mark is 0.5 degrees. The top of the red column is 1 tick mark below −1: −1.5 °C. (Counting each tick mark as 0.1 gives −1.1.)

items.q: Which describes where −2.7 is on a number line?
items.e: −2.7 is 2.7 units left of 0, past −2 but not as far as −3. It is 0.3 from −3 and 0.7 from −2, so it is between −3 and −2, closer to −3.

sets.title: Compare and order fractions and decimals

items.q: Which statement is true?
items.e: −0.25 is closer to 0 than −0.5, so −0.25 > −0.5. The others are false: 0.45 < 0.50, −0.8 < −0.75 and −1.2 < −1.15.

items.q: Which statement is true?
items.e: 0.5 = 0.50, and 45 hundredths < 50 hundredths, so 0.45 < 0.5. A longer decimal is not always greater. The others are false: −0.5 is farther left than −0.25, −0.06 is closer to 0 than −0.6, and 0.305 < 0.350.

items.q: Which statement is true?
Which statement is true?
items.e: −0.06 is 6 hundredths from 0. −0.6 = −0.60 is 60 hundredths from 0, farther left. So −0.06 > −0.6. The others are false: −1.2 = −1.20 < −1.15, 0.305 < 0.350, and 0.45 < 0.50.

items.q: Which statement is true?
items.e: Write −2.4 as −2.400. −2.375 is closer to 0, so −2.375 > −2.4. The others are false: 0.09 < 0.10, −0.8 < −0.75 and −0.5 < −0.25.

items.q: Which number is the least? −0.6, −0.65, −0.065, 0.6
items.e: The least number is the one farthest left on a number line: −0.65. −0.65 = −0.650 is farther from 0 than −0.6 = −0.600 and −0.065.

items.q: Which number is the greatest? −34, −23, −0.7, −0.72
items.e: Write the fractions as decimals: −34 = −0.75; −23 = about −0.667. All four are negative, so the greatest is the one closest to 0: −23.

items.q: Which number is the greatest? −1.09, −1.9, −1.1, −1.009
items.e: All four are negative, so the greatest is the one closest to 0: −1.009. −1.9 has the biggest digits, so it is the least.

items.q: Which number is the least? −2 12, −2.45, −2 38, −2.4
items.e: Write the fractions as decimals: −2 12 = −2.5; −2 38 = −2.375. The least number is the one farthest left on a number line: −2 12. −2.5 = −2.50 is farther from 0 than −2.45.

items.q: Which number is the greatest? 0.408, 0.48, 0.4, 0.084
items.e: Compare place by place: 0.480 is the most thousandths. The greatest is 0.48. 0.408 has more digits, but 0.408 < 0.480.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest? −0.5, −0.25, 0.4, −0.75
items.e: Start with the number farthest left. Among negative numbers, the one farthest from 0 is the least: −0.75, −0.5, −0.25, 0.4.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest? −12, −13, −34, 23
c: −34, −12, −13, 23
23, −13, −12, −34
−13, −12, −34, 23
−13, −12, 23, −34
items.e: Write the fractions as decimals: −12 = −0.5; −13 = about −0.333; −34 = −0.75; 23 = about 0.667. Start with the number farthest left. Among negative numbers, the one farthest from 0 is the least: −34, −12, −13, 23.

items.q: Which list is in order from least to greatest? −1.2, 0.8, −1.25, −0.08
items.e: Start with the number farthest left. Among negative numbers, the one farthest from 0 is the least: −1.25, −1.2, −0.08, 0.8.

items.q: Which list is in order from greatest to least? −25, 0.3, −0.45, −14
c: −0.45, −25, −14, 0.3
−0.45, −25, 0.3, −14
0.3, −0.45, −25, −14
0.3, −14, −25, −0.45
items.e: Write the fractions as decimals: −25 = −0.4; −14 = −0.25. Start with the number farthest right. Among negative numbers, the one closest to 0 comes first: 0.3, −14, −25, −0.45.

items.q: Which list is in order from greatest to least? −3.6, −3 34, −3.06, 3.5
items.e: Write the fractions as decimals: −3 34 = −3.75. Start with the number farthest right. Among negative numbers, the one closest to 0 comes first: 3.5, −3.06, −3.6, −3 34.

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: −23 < −34
−23 > −34
23 > 34
−23 = −34
items.e: Use a common denominator: −23 = −812 and −34 = −912. −812 is closer to 0, so −23 > −34. Without the signs it is the other way: 23 < 34.

items.q: Which statement is true?
items.e: 58 = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, so −58 = −0.625. It is farther from 0 than −0.600, so −58 < −0.6.

items.q: Which statement is true?
items.e: 38 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, so 38 = 0.375. 0.38 is close, but it is not equal: 0.375 rounds to 0.38.

items.q: Which temperature is the coldest? −2.5 °C, −2.05 °C, −2.45 °C, −0.25 °C
items.e: The coldest temperature is the least number, the one farthest below 0. −2.5 = −2.50 is farther below 0 than −2.45 and −2.05: −2.5 °C.

items.q: Which temperature is warmer than −4.3 °C?
items.e: Warmer means greater: closer to 0 or above it. −4.25 is closer to 0 than −4.3 = −4.30, so −4.25 °C is warmer. −4.35, −4.5 and −4.31 are all colder.

items.q: Write 68 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 6 and 8 is 2. 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so 68 = 34. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number.

items.q: Write 912 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 9 and 12 is 3. 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 912 = 34. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number.

items.q: Write 1218 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 12 and 18 is 6. 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so 1218 = 23. (Dividing by 2 gives 69: equal, but not yet in simplest form.)

items.q: Write 1525 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 15 and 25 is 5. 15 ÷ 5 = 3 and 25 ÷ 5 = 5, so 1525 = 35. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number.

items.q: Write 1624 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 16 and 24 is 8. 16 ÷ 8 = 2 and 24 ÷ 8 = 3, so 1624 = 23. (Dividing by 2 gives 812: equal, but not yet in simplest form.)

items.q: Write 1435 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 14 and 35 is 7. 14 ÷ 7 = 2 and 35 ÷ 7 = 5, so 1435 = 25. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number.

items.q: Write 2032 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 20 and 32 is 4. 20 ÷ 4 = 5 and 32 ÷ 4 = 8, so 2032 = 58. (Dividing by 2 gives 1016: equal, but not yet in simplest form.)

items.q: Write 1845 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 18 and 45 is 9. 18 ÷ 9 = 2 and 45 ÷ 9 = 5, so 1845 = 25. (Dividing by 3 gives 615: equal, but not yet in simplest form.)

items.q: Write −1015 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 10 and 15 is 5. 10 ÷ 5 = 2 and 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so −1015 = −23. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number. Keep the minus sign.

items.q: Write −812 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 8 and 12 is 4. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so −812 = −23. (Dividing by 2 gives −46: equal, but not yet in simplest form.) Keep the minus sign.

items.q: Write −2128 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 21 and 28 is 7. 21 ÷ 7 = 3 and 28 ÷ 7 = 4, so −2128 = −34. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number. Keep the minus sign.

items.q: Write −2440 in simplest form.
items.e: The greatest common factor (GCF) of 24 and 40 is 8. 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 40 ÷ 8 = 5, so −2440 = −35. (Dividing by 2 gives −1220: equal, but not yet in simplest form.) Keep the minus sign.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor of 24 and 36?
items.e: Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The greatest one in both lists is 12. 6 and 4 are common factors, but not the greatest. 72 is a common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor of 18 and 30?
items.e: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. The greatest one in both lists is 6. 90 is a common multiple, not a factor.

items.q: Which fraction is in simplest form?
items.e: A fraction is in simplest form when the only common factor of the numerator and the denominator is 1. 9 = 3 × 3 and 16 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 share no factor, so 916 is in simplest form. 615 (÷ 3), 1421 (÷ 7) and 1012 (÷ 2) can be simplified.

items.q: Which fraction is in simplest form?
items.e: 5 and 9 have no common factor except 1, so −59 is in simplest form. −410 (÷ 2), −915 (÷ 3) and −1216 (÷ 4) can be simplified.

items.q: Write 0.75 as a fraction in simplest form.
items.e: 0.75 is 75 hundredths = 75100. Divide both parts by 25: 34.

items.q: Write −0.4 as a fraction in simplest form.
items.e: 0.4 is 4 tenths = 410. Divide both parts by 2: 25. With the sign: −25.

items.q: Write −0.6 as a fraction in simplest form.
items.e: 0.6 is 6 tenths = 610. Divide both parts by 2: 35. With the sign: −35.

items.q: Write 0.35 as a fraction in simplest form.
items.e: 0.35 is 35 hundredths = 35100. Divide both parts by 5: 720.

items.q: Which number is between 0.3 and 0.4?
items.e: 0.3 = 0.30 and 0.4 = 0.40. Any number of hundredths from 31 to 39 is between them: 0.37.

items.q: Which number is between −0.5 and −0.4?
items.e: Write them as −0.50 and −0.40. −0.45 is halfway between them: −0.45. −0.55 is farther left than −0.5.

items.q: Which number is between −2 and −2.1?
items.e: Write them as −2.00 and −2.10. −2.05 is between them: −2.05. −2.5 is farther left than −2.1.

items.q: Which number is between 14 and 13?
items.e: 14 = 0.25 and 13 = 0.333… So 0.3 is between them. 0.25 is equal to 14, so it is not between.

items.q: Which number is between −34 and −12?
items.e: Use eighths: −34 = −68 and −12 = −48. −58 is between them: −58.

items.q: Which number is between −12 and −13?
items.e: Use twelfths: −12 = −612 and −13 = −412. −512 is between them: −512.

items.q: Which number is between −0.1 and −0.09?
items.e: Write them as −0.100 and −0.090. −0.095 is between them: −0.095. Adding a thousandths digit gives room for more numbers.

items.q: Which number is not between −3 and −2?
items.e: −3.2 is farther left than −3, so −3.2 is not between −3 and −2. The other three are all more than −3 and less than −2.

items.q: Which number is exactly halfway between −0.6 and −0.5?
items.e: Write them as −0.60 and −0.50. Halfway between 60 and 50 hundredths is 55 hundredths: −0.55.

items.q: Which statement about 0.12 and 0.13 is true?
c: There are many numbers between them, such as 0.125.
There are no numbers between them.
items.e: Between any two different numbers there is always another number. 0.12 = 0.120 and 0.13 = 0.130, so 0.121, 0.125 and 0.1255 are all between them. There are many numbers between them.

items.q: Round 3.648 to the nearest hundredth.
items.e: To the nearest hundredth, look at the thousandths digit: 8. It is 5 or more, so round up: 3.65.

items.q: Round 5.555 to the nearest tenth.
items.e: To the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: 5. It is 5 or more, so round up: 5.6.

items.q: Round 0.047 to the nearest hundredth.
items.e: To the nearest hundredth, look at the thousandths digit: 7. It is 5 or more, so round up: 0.05.

items.q: Round 0.666 to the nearest hundredth.
items.e: To the nearest hundredth, look at the thousandths digit: 6. It is 5 or more, so round up: 0.67. 0.667 is rounded to the nearest thousandth, not hundredth.

items.q: Round −2.46 to the nearest tenth.
items.e: Round 2.46 as if it were positive. To the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: 6. It is 5 or more, so 2.46 rounds to 2.5. Keep the minus sign: −2.5.

items.q: Round −0.38 to the nearest tenth.
items.e: Round 0.38 as if it were positive. To the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: 8. It is 5 or more, so 0.38 rounds to 0.4. Keep the minus sign: −0.4. −0.38 is closer to −0.4 than to −0.3.

items.q: Round −14.7 to the nearest whole number.
items.e: Round 14.7 as if it were positive. To the nearest whole number, look at the tenths digit: 7. It is 5 or more, so 14.7 rounds to 15. Keep the minus sign: −15.

items.q: Round 12.49 to the nearest whole number.
items.e: To the nearest whole number, look at the tenths digit: 4. It is 4 or less, so round down: 12. Do not round twice (12.49 → 12.5 → 13). Use the digit right after the ones place.

items.q: Round −6.97 to the nearest tenth.
items.e: Round 6.97 as if it were positive. To the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: 7. It is 5 or more, so 6.97 rounds to 7.0. Keep the minus sign: −7.0. 9 tenths + 1 tenth = 10 tenths = 1 one, so 6.9 becomes 7.0. Keep the 0 to show tenths.

items.q: Which number rounds to −3.2 when it is rounded to the nearest tenth?
items.e: −3.18 is 2 hundredths from −3.2, so it rounds to −3.2: −3.18. −3.12 rounds to −3.1, −3.26 rounds to −3.3, and 3.18 is positive.

sets.title: Word problems: temperatures, lake levels and more

items.q: The water level of a lake dropped to 0.75 m below its normal level. Which number shows the water level compared with normal?
items.e: Below the normal level is the negative direction, and 0 is the normal level. The level is −0.75 (in metres).

items.q: At the Terry Fox Run, Maya ran 2.75 km and Arjun ran 2 34 km. Which statement is true?
c: A fraction and a decimal cannot be compared.
items.e: 34 = 0.75, so 2 34 km = 2.75 km. They ran the same distance.

items.q: In Owen’s class, 38 of the students walk to school and 0.4 of the students take the bus. Which statement is true?
c: More students take the bus than walk.
The same number of students walk and take the bus.
A fraction and a decimal cannot be compared.
More students walk than take the bus.
items.e: 38 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, and 0.375 < 0.400. More students take the bus than walk.

items.q: Ethan’s bank balance is −$12.50. Chloe’s bank balance is −$12.05. Who owes more money?
items.e: A negative balance is money owed. $12.50 is more than $12.05, so −$12.50 is farther below $0. Ethan owes more.

items.q: One night in January, the lows were: Kenora −8.45 °C, Timmins −8.5 °C, Sudbury −8.05 °C, Thunder Bay −8.4 °C. Which town was the coldest?
items.e: The coldest is the least number. Write them with two decimal places: −8.45, −8.50, −8.05, −8.40. −8.50 is farthest below 0, so Timmins was the coldest.

items.q: Near a wharf in Nova Scotia, a scuba diver is at −4.25 m, a crab is at −4.5 m and a lobster trap is at −4.05 m. The dock is at 1.5 m. (0 m is sea level.) Which is the lowest?
items.e: The lowest is the least number. −4.5 = −4.50 is farther below 0 than −4.25 and −4.05, so the crab is the lowest.

items.q: Luge races are timed to the thousandth of a second. At a youth race in Calgary, the times were: Mei 48.37 s, Kai 48.4 s, Zoe 48.307 s, Mateo 48.73 s. Who was the fastest?
items.e: The fastest slider has the least time. Write them with three decimal places: 48.370, 48.400, 48.307, 48.730. 48.307 is the least, so Zoe was the fastest.

items.q: The overnight low in Barrie was between −6.3 °C and −6.2 °C. Which temperature could it have been?
items.e: Write them as −6.30 and −6.20. −6.25 is between them: −6.25 °C.

items.q: A recipe for maple syrup cookies needs more than 13 cup of syrup but less than 12 cup. Which amount works?
items.e: 13 = 0.333… and 12 = 0.5. 0.4 cup is between them. 0.3 is less than 0.333…

items.q: An arena manager wants the ice temperature between −5.5 °C and −4.5 °C. Which reading is in that range?
items.e: −4.75 is more than −5.5 and less than −4.5, so −4.75 °C is in the range. −5.75 is too cold and −4.25 is too warm.

items.q: 18 of the 24 students in Priya’s class went to the skating rink. What fraction of the class went, in simplest form?
items.e: 1824: the GCF of 18 and 24 is 6. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so 34. 14 is the part that did not go.

items.q: Leah’s ringette team won 12 of its 20 games. What fraction of the games did the team win, in simplest form?
items.e: 1220: the GCF of 12 and 20 is 4. 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 35. 25 is the part of the games they lost.

items.q: Gas costs 151.9¢ per litre. What is that price rounded to the nearest cent?
items.e: Look at the tenths digit: 9. It is 5 or more, so round up: 152¢. 151¢ cuts off the 9 instead of rounding.

items.q: A thermometer in Iqaluit reads −17.6 °C. What is the temperature to the nearest degree?
items.e: Round 17.6 as if it were positive: the tenths digit is 6, so it rounds up to 18. Keep the sign: −18 °C. −17.6 is closer to −18 than to −17.

items.q: A research submarine in Lake Superior is at −87.46 m (0 m is the surface of the lake). What is its position to the nearest tenth of a metre?
items.e: Look at the hundredths digit: 6. It is 5 or more, so 87.46 rounds to 87.5. Keep the sign: −87.5 m.

items.q: The CN Tower in Toronto is about 553.33 m tall. What is its height to the nearest tenth of a metre?
items.e: Look at the hundredths digit: 3. It is 4 or less, so round down: 553.3 m. 553 is rounded to the nearest whole metre.

items.q: The water level in a rain barrel changed by −38 m in week 1 and by −25 m in week 2. Which statement is true?
c: The level dropped more in week 1.
The level dropped the same amount both weeks.
The level dropped more in week 2.
items.e: −38 = −0.375 and −25 = −0.4. −0.400 is farther below 0 than −0.375, so the level dropped more in week 2.

items.q: In March, Lake Ontario was 0.08 m below its average level. In April, it was 0.12 m below. Which statement is true?
c: Both months were at the same level.
items.e: Below average is negative: March −0.08, April −0.12. −0.12 is farther below 0, so April was lower: −0.12 < −0.08.

items.q: One January afternoon the temperatures were: Toronto −3.5 °C, Ottawa −8.25 °C, Montréal −8.5 °C, Halifax 3.75 °C. Which list goes from warmest to coldest?
items.e: Warmest is the greatest number. 3.75 is the only positive temperature. Then −3.5, then −8.25, and −8.5 = −8.50 is the coldest: Halifax, Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal.

items.q: In gym class, Liam ran the 60 m dash in 9.4 s and Owen ran it in 9.5 s. Hana’s time was between their times. Which could be Hana’s time?
items.e: Write them as 9.40 and 9.50. 9.45 is between them: 9.45 s. 9.045 is less than 9.4.
